subject: biology
title: Risk factors and lifestyle in non-communicable disease
key_idea: Risk factors are linked to an increased rate of a disease. Diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol all affect non-communicable diseases, and many diseases are caused by several factors interacting. BMI and waist-to-hip ratio help to judge weight and health. These diseases cost people and nations a great deal.

blocks.text: This section covers what a risk factor is and how several factors can combine to cause one disease.

items.meaning: Something linked to an increased rate of a disease. It may be an aspect of lifestyle, or a substance in the body or environment.
A substance or radiation, such as ionising radiation, that can cause cancer.

items: A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not for others.
Many non-communicable diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors. Examples are cardiovascular disease, cancer, bronchitis and liver disease.
Medical risk factors for coronary heart disease include high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes and genetic factors.
Lifestyle risk factors include smoking, obesity, lack of exercise, a high fat diet, a lot of salt and alcohol.
A risk factor is linked to a higher rate of a disease. It does not always cause it.
Several factors often interact to cause a disease.
Link each factor to its effect, for example smoking to high blood pressure and fatty deposits.

blocks.text: Diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol each affect particular diseases. Learn the main links.

rows: A high fat diet raises cholesterol and can cause fatty deposits and cardiovascular disease. Obesity is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes.
Lack of exercise raises the risk of obesity, high blood pressure, diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
Raises blood pressure, cholesterol and fatty deposits, so raises the risk of cardiovascular disease. Also causes lung disease and lung cancer. Smoking in pregnancy affects the unborn baby.
Affects the liver and brain function. Alcohol in pregnancy affects the unborn baby.

items: Diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol all affect the rate of non-communicable disease.
Obesity is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

blocks.text: BMI and waist-to-hip ratio are used to find out if a person is obese. BMI uses mass and height.

diagram.alt: A BMI calculation with new numbers each time.
diagram.question: A person has a mass of {mass} kg and a height of {height} m. Calculate their BMI. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

blocks.label: Waist-to-hip ratio
blocks.formula: waist-to-hip ratio = waist measurement ÷ hip measurement
where: waist and hip measured in the same unit, such as cm

items: Interpreting BMI: below 18.5 is underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 is healthy, 25.0 to 29.9 is overweight and 30.0 and above is obese.
Waist-to-hip ratio shows where weight is carried. A high ratio means more fat around the abdomen. A male with a ratio above 0.90 is abdominally obese.
Someone can be overweight by BMI but not abdominally obese, if the weight is spread over the body.
BMI = mass in kg ÷ (height in m)².
Waist-to-hip ratio shows weight distribution. BMI does not.

blocks.text: Non-communicable diseases have human and financial costs. These fall on individuals, local communities, nations and the world.

items: An individual may have movement problems, lose a job or income, or suffer mental health effects.
They may need to visit the doctor, take medication regularly or have surgery.
Communities and nations pay for treatment and lose the work of ill people.
Diseases caused by lifestyle factors are found at local, national and global levels.
Costs are both human (health, lifestyle) and financial (treatment, lost income).
They affect individuals, communities, nations and the world.

checks.q: A person has a mass of 72 kg and a height of 1.81 m. Calculate their BMI to 3 significant figures.
Give two ways that smoking can affect health.
checks.a: Any two from: lung cancer, lung disease, increased blood pressure, increased risk of heart (cardiovascular) disease.

checks.q: A person has a BMI of 28.5. Explain one way they could change their lifestyle to reach a healthy weight.
checks.a: Do more exercise, so more energy is used up. Or eat less fat or carbohydrate, so energy intake is reduced.

smoking: high bp / cholesterol / fatty deposition
high salt intake: high blood pressure

mistakes.wrong: A disease related to being overweight is obesity.
mistakes.right: "Obesity" is ignored when asked for a disease related to being overweight. Name the disease, such as type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure or cancer.

mistakes.wrong: Only lifestyle risk factors are given for CHD.
mistakes.right: For top marks give both lifestyle and medical factors, and link them: for example smoking raises blood pressure, and obesity links to high cholesterol and fatty deposition.

mistakes.wrong: A heart attack is a disease caused by being overweight.
mistakes.right: "Heart attack" and "heart failure" are ignored. Name coronary heart disease or cardiovascular disease.

worked_example.question: Coronary heart disease (CHD) is a non-communicable disease. CHD is caused when fatty material builds up in the coronary arteries. Explain how lifestyle and medical risk factors increase the chance of developing CHD.
answer_points: Medical risk factors: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, genetic factors, medications.
Lifestyle risk factors: smoking, obesity, lack of exercise, a high fat or high energy diet, too little fruit and vegetables, alcohol, high salt intake.
Link the factors: smoking increases blood pressure, cholesterol and fatty deposition.
Obesity links to lack of exercise, high blood pressure, cholesterol, fatty deposition and diabetes.
A diet high in fat links to obesity, cholesterol and diabetes. High salt intake links to high blood pressure.
Genetic factors link to blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes and obesity.
worked_example.tip: The main discriminator is the quality of linking. Both lifestyle and medical factors are needed for the top level.

exam_phrases: waist : hip ratio above 0.90: abdominally obese
BMI shows overweight but not abdominally obese
do more exercise, so more energy is used up
reduce fat / carbohydrate intake, so energy intake is reduced

mistakes.right: Height is squared: BMI = mass in kilograms ÷ (height in metres)².
Read the rounding instruction. To 3 significant figures, 21.977 is 22.0. A correct evaluation without rounding loses the last mark.

mistakes.wrong: Do more exercise to lose weight.
mistakes.right: Add the reason: so more energy is used up. One mark is for the change, one for what it does.

worked_example.question: BMI is calculated using the equation: BMI = mass in kilograms ÷ (height in metres)². Male B has a mass of 72 kg and a height of 1.81 m. Calculate the BMI of male B. Give the answer to 3 significant figures.
worked_example.tip: A correct numerical answer with no working gets full marks. Write the working anyway, in case of a slip.

exam_phrases: the more points a person scores, the higher the risk
total the points for each person
Person A has a greater risk
correct deduction based on the total of points

mistakes.wrong: Person A is most likely to get CHD.
mistakes.right: Show the working. Total the points for each person (Person A 8, Person B 7), then state which total is higher.

mistakes.wrong: Only one risk factor, such as smoking, is used to decide who is at more risk.
mistakes.right: Use every row of the table. CHD risk comes from several factors, so add up the points for all of them.

worked_example.question: A table is used to estimate the risk of getting CHD. The more points a person scores, the higher the risk. Age: under 20 is 1 point, 21 to 30 is 2 points, 31 to 40 is 3 points. Blood cholesterol: low 1, medium 2, high 3. Cigarettes per day: 0 is 1 point, 1 to 10 is 2 points, 11 to 20 is 3 points. Mass: below average 1, average 2, above average 3. Parents with CHD: 0 is 1 point, 1 is 2 points, 2 is 3 points. Person A: 25 years old, non-smoker, low blood cholesterol, average mass, one parent with CHD. Person B: 19 years old, smokes 20 cigarettes a day, low blood cholesterol, below average mass, no parents with CHD. Use the table to work out whether Person A or Person B is most likely to develop CHD. Show how you worked out your answer.
answer_points: Person A has a total of 8 points.
Person B has a total of 7 points.
Person A has a greater risk.
worked_example.tip: Show each total. A correct deduction from your own totals is still credited if there is a slip in adding up the points.
